content: Neonatal tetanus is a specific form of generalized tetanus that affects newborns. It occurs in infants who have not received passive immunity from their mothers, particularly when the mother has not been immunized against tetanus. The infection typically arises from the contamination of the unhealed umbilical stump, especially when it is cut with non-sterile instruments. This condition is most prevalent in developing countries with underdeveloped healthcare systems and is rare in developed nations. Neonatal tetanus is caused by the bacterium Clostridium tetani. The spores of this bacterium are ubiquitous in the environment, making immunization the only effective preventive measure. Women of childbearing age are advised to receive three properly spaced doses of the tetanus toxoid vaccine, either before or during pregnancy, to protect their future babies from neonatal tetanus. Symptoms of neonatal tetanus typically manifest between 4 to 14 days after birth, with an average onset around 7 days. The fatality rate for affected infants is alarmingly high, ranging from 70% to 100%, with death often occurring by the age of two weeks. Clinical findings have identified four distinct forms of tetanus, and the time from exposure to symptom onset can extend to several months. Common clinical signs include an unhealed, unhygienic umbilical stump, trismus (spasm of the masseter muscles), risus sardonicus (spasm of facial muscles), clenched hands, dorsiflexion of the feet, and opisthotonus (spasm of spinal muscles). In 2000, neonatal tetanus accounted for approximately 14% of all neonatal deaths, equating to 215,000 fatalities. By 2008, the number of deaths had decreased to 59,000 worldwide. In 2005, 57 countries were identified as still being at risk, with 27 countries accounting for 90% of cases. By December 2013, the number of at-risk countries had been reduced to 25. The World Health Congress in 1989 called for the elimination of neonatal tetanus, with UNICEF leading the initiative alongside other United Nations agencies, governments, and non-profit organizations. By 2000, the disease was declared eliminated in 104 of 161 developing countries. Elimination is defined as fewer than one case per 1,000 live births in every district of a country. The campaign was later expanded to target both maternal and neonatal tetanus, as postpartum mothers are also at risk. Public health efforts have focused on education about hygienic birth practices, infant cord care, and the importance of immunization, particularly targeting pregnant women. In Egypt, neonatal tetanus cases dropped from 4,000 to fewer than 500 annually due to an immunization campaign. In Morocco, neonatal tetanus accounted for 20% of neonatal deaths in 1987 but only 2% by 1992. In Uganda, 3,433 cases of neonatal tetanus were recorded in 1998, with 2,403 resulting in death. However, after significant public health efforts, Uganda was certified as having eliminated tetanus in 2011. In Yemen, UNICEF partnered with Pampers in 2011 to address maternal and neonatal tetanus. Kiwanis International pledged $110 million in 2010 to eliminate maternal and neonatal tetanus globally in partnership with UNICEF. India was declared free of maternal and neonatal tetanus by the World Health Organization (WHO) on May 15, 2015. This achievement was announced by Prime Minister Narendra Modi during the Call to Action Summit in New Delhi on August 27, 2015. India reduced its infant mortality rate (IMR) from 380 in 1990 to 40 in 2015 and its maternal mortality rate (MMR) from 540 to 167 during the same period. The national health program, initiated in 1983, provided all pregnant women with two doses of the tetanus vaccine. As a result, deaths from tetanus in India dropped from 79,000 in 1990 to fewer than 500 in 2013 and 2014.
